newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ parties avoid blank cheque promises - economist.
newsitem.headline: NZ parties avoid blank cheque promises - economist.

text.p: New Zealand political parties have largely avoided making expensive blank cheque promises in presenting fiscal projections ahead of the October 12 election, private forecaster Infometrics said on Wednesday.
"The parties have generally been sensitive to ensure they show the cost of the promises they make," economist Philip Wrigley said in an economic analysis of the parties' promises.
The left-wing Alliance Party is the big spender with plans to boost current expenditure projections by NZ$4.8 billion in 1997/98 compared with the current National Party government.
Left-of-centre Labour Party would spend $2.4 billion more and the economic nationalist New Zealand First $1.7 billion.
Even the ruling conservative National Party would increase spending beyond current baselines based on recent patterns.
Although the Alliance is the big spender, it also promises to be the biggest saver as a result of tax increases, with an estimated surplus of $3.7 billion in fiscal 1997/98.
Infometrics estimates all parties will run surpluses for that year, with Labour having the smallest at $1.66 billion.
"It gambles that much lower surpluses will support growth as well as National's plan," he said.
But he warns there could be a monetary policy response from the Reserve Bank to Labour's shrinking surpluses.
NZ First faces the challenge of achieving growth to pay for its spending but its plans for a compulsory pension scheme should avoid inflation pressures, Wrigley said.
Plans by NZ First and the Alliance to introduce specific restrictions on foreign investment may have significant impact.

Wrigley said the main question mark the Alliance faces is not over the detail of costings, but whether the economic framework it would create would deliver a prosperous economy able to generate the tax revenues its plans require.
He is critical of its plan to amend the Reserve Bank Act so the central bank's targets include sustainable economic well-being and employment, together with price stability.
"The Reserve Bank cannout pursue all these objectives using the tools of monetary policy. Therefore, it is unlikely to achieve any consistently," Wrigley said.
Labour plans to cut taxes and raise spending substantially.
Only the Alliance proposes to restrict free trade and its plans to raise $1 billion via a "moderate" increase in tariffs against all countries but Australia could result in conterveiling measures.
Wrigley sees conflicts within all parties' policies:
* The Alliance's proposals for trade restrictions and multiple objectives for monetary policy do not accord with accepted economic principles.
* NZ First has an incompatibility between its "partnership with exporters" and constraints on foreign investment.
* Labour is accused of reducing flexibility in employment contracting
* National proffers an ambitious growth target without suggesting reforms to achieve it.
Polls suggest no party will achieve an overall majority in the election and Wrigley said "all four would have to swallow hard to accept key planks of any of the other parties".
As none of the parties would rule alone, Wrigley suspects much of the fiscal policies "represent bargaining positions for post-election negotiations as much as enticements for voters".
